summary: Describes how to put CBOR Web Token (CWT) claims into the header parameters of any COSE structure. This lets some claims be read before decryption or without inspecting a detached payload.

eli5.summary: Putting the sender's name on the outside of a sealed envelope lets you read it without opening the envelope. This does that for CWT claims.

questions: what is the cwt claims header parameter
why put cwt claims in a cose header
subtitle: A COSE header parameter that carries CWT claims outside the payload, readable before decryption.

tldr.problem: CWT claims normally sit in the COSE payload, so they are hidden when the payload is encrypted or detached, and cannot be used when the payload is not a CWT Claims Set at all.
tldr.mechanism: A new COSE header parameter, CWT Claims (label 15), holds a map of CWT claims in the protected or unprotected header of any COSE structure.
tldr.outcome: Applications can read selected claims, such as an issuer for key discovery, before decryption or without inspecting a detached payload.

facts.label: Occurrences
facts.value: Once, in protected or unprotected header

today: RFC 9597 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2024, and the data supplied for this RFC lists no obsoleting or updating documents. It registers the CWT Claims header parameter in the IANA COSE Header Parameters registry.

sections.title: Why Claims in Headers
sections.content:
Some uses of COSE need a standard place for CWT claims ([RFC8392]) in the header parameters. These include encrypted COSE structures, structures with a detached signature, and payloads that are not CWT Claims Sets, even payloads that are not CBOR at all. For example, an application might put an iss (issuer) claim in a COSE_Sign1 structure whose payload is a bitmap image, and use the issuer value for key discovery.

JWT already had this: Section 5.3 of RFC 7519 lets selected claims appear as JOSE header parameters so they stay visible even when the JWT is encrypted. No equivalent was standardized for CWTs, and this specification corrects that omission.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the important label, like who sent it, is locked inside the package. This lets you also put that label on the outside.

sections.title: A Single Header Parameter
sections.content:
Putting claim values directly into the header would not work, because the numeric header parameter assignments conflict with the numeric CWT claim assignments. Instead, the RFC defines one header parameter, CWT Claims, with label 15 and a map value whose keys come from the CWT Claims registry. A non-normative CDDL description gives it as a map of Claim-Label (an integer or text) to any value.

The parameter MAY be used in any COSE object that uses header parameters, such as COSE_Sign objects, and is not restricted to CWTs. The RFC does not define what the claims mean for a particular application.
sections.eli5: Instead of mixing the labels in with the other outside labels, there is one special pocket on the outside, and the claims go inside that pocket.

sections.title: Processing Rules
sections.content:
If the same claims appear in both the payload and the header of a CWT, the receiving application MUST verify that their values are identical, unless it defines other specific processing rules. This avoids confusion from different values for the same claim.

It is RECOMMENDED to use the parameter only in a protected header so the contents cannot be altered, and it MUST occur only once in either the protected or the unprotected header of a COSE structure.

Because understanding the claims needs a known interpretation, that information MAY come from other header parameters. Where no natural way exists, using the typ header parameter from RFC 9596 is RECOMMENDED. Recipients MUST NOT use the claims beyond the integrity protection or authentication given to the parameter and to the information used to derive its interpretation.
sections.eli5: If the outside label and the inside letter both say who sent it, they must say the same thing. And the outside label is best stamped so nobody can change it.

sections.title: Privacy and Security
sections.content:
CWT claims in COSE headers are not encrypted, and some registered claims may hold privacy-sensitive information. Applications should make such objects visible only to parties allowed to see that information.

Implementers should review Section 8 of RFC 8392. With detached content, the application is responsible for transporting it unchanged, as described in RFC 9052. Acting on claims before their integrity is cryptographically verified is risky, whether they are in the payload or a header, so tentative decisions must be confirmed once cryptographic processing completes. That includes information used to work out the claims' interpretation.
sections.eli5: Anything on the outside of the envelope can be read by anyone, so do not put secrets there, and double-check it once you open the envelope.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: IANA registered the new COSE header parameter CWT Claims in the COSE Header Parameters registry. Table 1 of the RFC gives its label as 15, its value type as map, and its value registry as the map keys in the CWT Claims registry, with the description "Location for CWT Claims in COSE Header Parameters".
sections.eli5: The official list of outside labels now has a spot reserved for this pocket.
